analysis.one_liner: Bans grocery price gouging, surveillance-based pricing, facial-recognition pricing, and electronic shelf labels.
analysis.headline: The bill has been referred to two House committees and has not moved since its August 2025 introduction, with 93 House Democrats cosponsoring it and no Republican support in the record.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for grocery stores to charge 'grossly excessive' prices, with an exception when the price reflects real costs the store cannot control. It would also stop stores from setting a person's price based on data collected about them — including facial recognition — require stores to post signs if they use facial recognition, and ban large stores from using electronic shelf labels that can change prices instantly. Enforcement would run through the Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits with minimum $3,000 damages, and the bill would bar stores from forcing customers into arbitration over these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers, especially lower-income households that spend a large share of their budget on groceries, would gain protection from excessive pricing and from personalized or surge pricing at the shelf. Consumers would also gain privacy protections: stores could not price them based on data gleaned from surveillance, could not use their biometric data without written consent, and would have to disclose facial recognition use at the entrance. People with claims against stores would keep access to court and class actions, since the bill voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these cases.

how_it_helps.text: Bars grocery stores from selling items at 'grossly excessive' prices, with the FTC to define the term — the bill suggests considering a threshold of 120% or more of the item's average market price over the prior six months; stores can defend a price by showing it reflects uncontrollable costs. [S2]

Prohibits 'surveillance-based price setting' — adjusting what a customer pays based on their personal information, including data collected through facial recognition or electronic shelf labels — while still allowing uniformly disclosed discounts for groups like seniors, students, and military members. [S2]

Requires stores using facial recognition to notify shoppers with clear signage at the entrance, and lets stores use biometric data only with written, informed consent and no sale or sharing with third parties. [S2]
Bans electronic shelf labels and digital price displays in stores larger than 10,000 square feet, requiring posted paper prices — aimed at technology that can change prices minute-to-minute. [S2]

Enforces the bans through the FTC, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits with at least $3,000 per violation (tripled for willful violations) plus attorney's fees, and makes pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for these claims. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Large grocery chains and other food retailers would bear the compliance costs: they could not deploy electronic shelf labels or surveillance-based pricing, would need signage and consent procedures for facial recognition, and would face FTC enforcement, state lawsuits, and private suits with $3,000-per-violation minimum damages. Suppliers of electronic shelf labels and retail data-analysis technology would lose a growing market in U.S. grocery stores.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large grocery chains and retail tech vendors

drawbacks.text: The price-gouging ban is vague by design: the FTC must define 'grossly excessive price' and 'market' after enactment, and a 120%-of-recent-average rule could flag ordinary price swings as violations, raising compliance costs that retailers may pass to shoppers. [S2]

The outright ban on electronic shelf labels in large stores would block a technology that can also post accurate unit prices, update sale prices quickly, and cut labor costs — opponents would argue it prevents efficiency gains and locks in older, costlier price-labeling methods. [S2]
The bill authorizes only $5 million for FTC implementation and enforcement, which may be thin for policing thousands of stores nationwide. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefits — protection from gouging and from being individually priced based on collected data — are real but depend heavily on FTC rulemaking that has not happened and may never. The costs fall on retailers and their technology vendors, and some compliance costs could reach shoppers through prices. The ban on electronic shelf labels is the bluntest tool in the bill: it addresses a real risk (minute-by-minute price changes) but also blocks efficiency gains, so the tradeoff there is genuinely debatable.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in August 2025 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, the bill has had no hearings, no markup, and no floor action since.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the bill on August 12, 2025, with 22 original cosponsors, all Democrats. [S2]
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Judiciary Committee. [S4]
93 House Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors appear in the record. [S3]
The full action history shows no further activity after the initial referral — no committee vote, no floor action. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, grocery retailers and retail-technology vendors are better off: with the bill stalled in committee, no pricing or labeling rules bind them, and no one has borne compliance costs or litigation risk.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Grocery chains, since nothing has passed

sides.party_line_note: Every named sponsor and all 93 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record, and with Republicans holding a House majority the bill faces an entirely one-sided path.

industries.industry: Large grocery and food retail chains
industries.note: The bill would bar chains larger than 10,000 square feet from electronic shelf labels and from setting prices based on shopper data, and expose them to price-gouging suits with $3,000-per-violation damages. Their interest in defeating it runs against shoppers' interest in stable, non-personalized prices.

industries.industry: Electronic shelf label and retail-surveillance technology vendors
industries.note: The bill bans electronic shelf labels in large grocery stores and restricts facial recognition and biometric data collection, cutting off a growing sales channel in U.S. food retail.

industries.industry: Data brokers and consumer-data analytics firms
industries.note: The bill's broad definition of personal information and its bar on surveillance-based pricing would restrict selling and using shopper data to set individualized grocery prices.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with two committees and has shown no movement since referral. First-term consumer-protection bills with purely Democratic support rarely get a hearing, let alone a floor vote, in a Republican-controlled House; the most likely path is that it dies quietly when this Congress ends in January 2027.
